entries.name: Neighbourhood components analysis
entries.definition: A supervised metric-learning algorithm that learns a linear transformation by maximizing the expected number of correctly classified training examples under stochastic leave-one-out neighbor selection.
entries.identity_notes: NCA is Goldberger et al.’s transformation-learning procedure, not ordinary k-nearest-neighbor voting or an unsupervised local-coordinate reconstruction. Its main objective sums correct-class probabilities; the paper also discusses a sum-of-log-probabilities alternative, which is a different objective. A rectangular transformation enables supervised dimensionality reduction. The AIO MetricLearning node is explicitly a deep neural network, so the original linear NCA procedure is not treated as its subclass. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 223 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Word-delimited fixed-string searches of both full checkouts, including ignored and hidden files, returned 2 worktree lines in discovery context and 6 main-checkout lines including four unrelated ignored dependency matches. Six neighboring native records and nine exact AIO nodes with scoped synonyms and outgoing edges were inspected.
limitations: Training uses class labels and a smooth stochastic surrogate, not the discontinuous deterministic k-nearest-neighbor accuracy. Improving its training objective does not certify held-out classification accuracy.

The objective is nonconvex in A; initialization and the optimizer affect its result. A=0 is a stationary point of the displayed gradient, so a claim that any initialization learns a useful metric would be unwarranted.

At least two observations are needed for the leave-one-out denominator. A class represented by a singleton has p_i=0 and contributes no correct-class reward; the paper’s logarithmic alternative is undefined for that point.

Rectangular or rank-deficient A yields a positive-semidefinite squared distance with possible collapsed directions. It need not define a strictly positive distance between distinct original points. No global optimum, absence of overfitting or benchmark advantage is asserted.

definition_evidence.locator: Sections 2–3, PDF pp. 1–4, Equations (1)–(7); rectangular projection and test-time classification at pp. 3–4

claims.statement: For labeled vectors x_i, choose a matrix A, possibly rectangular, and use squared transformed distance d_ij=||A(x_i−x_j)||², with Q=A^T A positive semidefinite. For j!=i set p_ij=exp(−d_ij)/sum_(k!=i)exp(−d_ik), and set p_ii=0. Define p_i=sum_(j:c_j=c_i)p_ij. Optimize f(A)=sum_i p_i by a gradient-based method; this is the expected number of correct labels when each training point selects one other point as its neighbor according to p_ij. For dimensionality reduction use A with d rows, store Ax_i and classify a new projected point using ordinary Euclidean k-nearest-neighbor voting. Learning the scale of A changes the softness of the training neighbor distribution; it does not uniquely determine the later integer k.

entries.name: Lifted structured embedding loss
entries.definition: A metric-learning objective that penalizes a positive pair’s Euclidean distance against negative distances incident to either endpoint, using a squared hinge and a hard maximum or its log-sum-exp relaxation.
entries.identity_notes: This record covers Song et al.’s lifted structured embedding loss, including the original maximum construction and the practically optimized log-sum-exp upper-bound form. These two forms are distinguished, not asserted numerically identical. The objective is separate from the full network, image preprocessing, hard-negative batch construction and optimizer. It is not N-pair-mc’s one-anchor dot-product categorical loss or N-pair-ovo’s sum of binary softplus comparisons. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 223 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Word-delimited fixed-string searches of both full checkouts, including ignored and hidden files, returned 2 worktree lines in discovery context and 6 main-checkout lines including four unrelated ignored dependency matches. Six neighboring native records and nine exact AIO nodes with scoped synonyms and outgoing edges were inspected.
limitations: The stated minibatch expression needs at least one positive pair and a nonempty negative pool for each evaluated pair. The paper’s loss definition does not itself provide an empty-batch fallback.

For a fixed candidate pool, log-sum-exp upper-bounds and smooths the inner maximum. It is not the same loss and depends on the number of negative terms. The Euclidean norm still requires care at zero distance when differentiating with respect to embeddings.

The original author loss file enumerates all same-label unordered pairs and both different-label endpoint pools in the supplied batch. That does not imply exhaustive mining over the whole training dataset or any particular sampling distribution.

This objective imposes neither a cosine normalization nor an InfoNCE positive-containing denominator. Margin, representation, batch composition and optimization affect results. No model training or benchmark was reproduced.

definition_evidence.locator: Section 4, PDF pp. 3–4 (printed 4006–4007), Equations (3)–(7), Algorithm 1; Section 5, PDF p. 5, implementation context

claims.statement: For labeled embeddings let D_ij=||z_i−z_j||_2. The original Equation (3) uses full-training-set positive pairs Phat and negative pairs Nhat. For positive (i,j), define J_ij=D_ij+max({alpha−D_ik:(i,k) in Nhat} union {alpha−D_jl:(j,l) in Nhat}), then average max(0,J_ij)^2 with divisor 2|Phat|. The practical Equation (4) instead uses a supplied minibatch: let P be its unordered same-class pairs and use Jtilde_ij=D_ij+log[sum_(k:y_k!=y_i)exp(alpha−D_ik)+sum_(l:y_l!=y_j)exp(alpha−D_jl)], summing only batch examples. Its loss is (1/(2|P|))sum_(i,j in P)max(0,Jtilde_ij)^2. Both endpoint-specific terms enter even when the same negative example belongs to both pools. Log-sum-exp bounds a hard maximum over the same terms; changing to a mined minibatch does not make its value a certified bound on the full-data objective. A dense pairwise distance matrix supports the batch computation. Loss distances are Euclidean norms, not squared distances; the squared matrix is only an intermediate.

entries.name: CURE clustering
entries.definition: An agglomerative clustering procedure that represents each cluster by several scattered points shrunk toward its mean and merges the pair with the smallest distance between their representative points.
entries.identity_notes: CURE uses a set of representative locations, unlike centroid-only k-means or graph-cut normalization in CHAMELEON. This record describes the original vector-data clustering rule and explicitly qualifies the faster representative-reuse and sampled-data enhancements. Recomputing representatives from all merged observations and selecting from old representatives need not give identical merges. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 223 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Word-delimited fixed-string searches of both full checkouts, including ignored and hidden files, returned 2 worktree lines in discovery context and 6 main-checkout lines including four unrelated ignored dependency matches. Six neighboring native records and nine exact AIO nodes with scoped synonyms and outgoing edges were inspected.
limitations: The mean-and-shrink description assumes a vector representation with a meaningful distance and arithmetic mean. The source’s mention of nonmetric similarities does not make the same operations defined for arbitrary categorical objects.

The improved representative-reuse step restricts the candidate set and can alter the selected representatives and later merges. Unshrinking from locations alone is undefined at alpha=1; it requires alpha<1 or retained original scattered points.

Sampling and partial partition clustering may miss rare groups or irreversibly combine points before the final pass. The paper’s two-stage small-cluster outlier removal is heuristic and can remove genuine small clusters.

Representative count, shrink fraction, sampling, partitioning, distance, outlier rules and target count matter. The method does not guarantee recovery of arbitrary true shapes or universal outlier robustness, and its indexing/runtime claims are dimension-dependent. No implementation or benchmark was reproduced.

definition_evidence.locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, PDF pp. 4–6 (printed 76–78), Figures 5–6 and improved merge procedure; Sections 4.1–4.4, PDF pp. 6–8, sampling, partitioning, labeling and outliers

claims.statement: Start with singleton clusters. Represent a cluster C by up to c selected points, with c a positive integer: choose the first farthest from its mean, then choose each next point to maximize its minimum distance to already selected points. Shrink every selected p to p+alpha(mean(C)−p), for a chosen shrink fraction in [0,1]. Define cluster distance as the minimum distance between a representative from each cluster, repeatedly merge the closest pair and stop at the requested count. In the original merge procedure recompute the mean with observation-count weights and select scattered points from the merged observations. The improved merge considers the at-most-2c old scattered points, recovered from their shrunken representatives when unshrinking is defined, and then shrinks new selections toward the merged mean. Large-data enhancements cluster a random sample, optionally partially cluster sample partitions before merging their partial clusters, and label remaining observations by the nearest selected final representative.

entries.name: ROCK clustering
entries.definition: An agglomerative clustering procedure that merges clusters using shared-neighbor link counts divided by a cluster-size normalization derived from a neighborhood model.
entries.identity_notes: ROCK is Guha et al.’s RObust Clustering using linKs procedure, designed for categorical or other similarity-based data. Links count common neighbors rather than direct similarities or graph cut weights. The normalized goodness is a heuristic and is not simply maximum shared-neighbor count. The record follows the 1999 conference article, not an uninspected expanded journal version. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 223 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Word-delimited fixed-string searches of both full checkouts, including ignored and hidden files, returned 2 worktree lines in discovery context and 6 main-checkout lines including four unrelated ignored dependency matches. Six neighboring native records and nine exact AIO nodes with scoped synonyms and outgoing edges were inspected.
limitations: The paper introduces a neighborhood-size model and chooses f(theta) for its experiments; the normalization is not a universal theorem for every supplied similarity or data distribution. theta=1 makes the displayed experimental-normalization denominator zero.

The graph and shared-neighbor counts depend on the supplied sample, similarity and threshold. Categorical attribute-value encoding with Jaccard similarity is one stated construction; shared-neighbor links do not guarantee semantic clustering.
The source’s prose explicitly allows termination above the requested count when all cross-links vanish. Forcing arbitrary zero-link merges changes that stopping convention.

Sampling and outlier details omitted from the conference article are deferred to its cited full report. This record does not invent those procedures or claim a benchmark/runtime advantage. No clustering implementation was executed.

definition_evidence.locator: Sections 3.1–3.3 and 4.1–4.6, PDF pp. 4–8 (printed 515–519), Figures 3–4; worked common-neighbor example in Section 3.2, p. 5; experimental f(theta) in Section 5, p. 8

claims.statement: On the clustering sample choose a symmetric similarity in [0,1] and threshold theta. Define N(i)={j!=i:sim(i,j)>=theta} and link(i,j)=|N(i) intersect N(j)|; excluding each point from its own neighbor list reproduces the paper’s worked link counts. For clusters A,B set Link(A,B)=sum_(i in A,j in B)link(i,j). Starting from singletons, merge the pair maximizing g(A,B)=Link(A,B)/[(|A|+|B|)^(1+2f)−|A|^(1+2f)−|B|^(1+2f)]. The paper’s experimental configuration uses f(theta)=(1−theta)/(1+theta); use 0<=theta<1 so f>0 and the denominator is positive. Update cross-cluster links additively after a merge. Stop at the requested cluster count or when every remaining cross-cluster link count is zero. The optional large-data procedure clusters a random sample and labels other observations using representative subsets L_i, choosing the cluster maximizing its threshold-neighbor count divided by (|L_i|+1)^f.
